newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao to appear at heavily-guarded court.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao to appear at heavily-guarded court.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, who launched economic reforms but was hobbled by corruption charges, will appear in a heavily-guarded court on Wednesday to face criminal forgery charges.

Hundreds of police and paramilitary troopers were expected to be deployed around a spacious international conference centre, where a special court room has been set up to handle two trials involving Rao, police said.

Rao's lawyer, R.K. Anand, said the former prime minister, 75, who served from mid-1991 to last May when his Congress party was defeated in general elections, would appear at the court shortly before 10 a.m. (0430 GMT).
Rao would be the first former or serving prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges.
Former prime minister Indira Gandhi was summoned to court in a civil case in 1977 after a state of emergency imposed by her ended.
Rao had been scheduled to appear in court in September.

But two cases -- one involving alleged forgery, the other criminal conspiracy to cheat -- became bogged down in procedural manoeuvres, and Rao has been spared the humiliation of either a court appearance or being taken into custody.

The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's federal police, on September 26 charged Rao and three others with involvement in an alleged attempt in 1989 to defame V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who later became prime minister.
They are alleged to have forged documents which aimed to show that Singh's son held $21 million in a bank account on the Caribbean island of St Kitts.
Rao has not commented publicly on the case.

He has been named but not formally charged in the 1983 cheating case. A hearing in the case is set for November 6 in the same court room. Both the forgery and cheating cases carry maximum penalties of seven years in jail.

Hundreds of journalists were expected to converge on the cavernous Vigyan Bhavan centre, chosen by police as a replacement site for crowded local courts where they feared an attack on the former prime minister.
Only 15 seats had been set aside for the media in the small court room, the United News of India said.
Rao stepped down as Congress leader in September after a local judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in the criminal cheating case.
But Rao, who said he was innocent of the charge of cheating a businessman out of $100,000 in 1983, has remained leader of Congress's parliamentary delegation and retains political clout.
His influence is magnified by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's dependence on Congress support to help thwart potential challenges from right-wing Hindu nationalists in parliament.
Deve Gowda's 13-party centre-left coalition does not control an outright majority in the lower house of parliament and needs Congress's backing.

Rao's lawyer Anand, said that at Wednesday's hearing, his team would press chief metropolitan magistrate Prem Kumar to extend the temporary bail that has protected Rao from arrest but which expires on November 6.
Anand was also expected to ask Kumar to exempt Rao from appearing in court during subsequent trial sessions, court officials said.
The CBI has also named Rao in a vote-buying case, which is still under investigation.
